subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OP WATERPOWERS IN ALBERTA, SASKATCHEWAN AND MANITOBA

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 311, respecting water-power in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OP WATERPOWERS IN ALBERTA, SASKATCHEWAN AND MANITOBA
speechtext:
Explain. The minister
said he proposed making a more lengthy statement.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OP WATERPOWERS IN ALBERTA, SASKATCHEWAN AND MANITOBA
speechtext:
This bill is to meet the request of the house formulated in a motion that the administration of water-powers alone should be transferred to the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and that these water-powers dhould be administered in the same manner as is provided for in the Railway Belt Waters Act, and under an agreement similar to that existing between the province of British Columbia and the Dominion government. In the case of British Columbia the Dominion government is the owner of the lands-the railway belt and the Peace River block. In the three provinces mentioned the ownership of the waters remains within the jurisdiction of the Dominion government. At first glance it would appear to be an easy matter to outline the provisions by statute and to declare in what manner this was to be done. The law officers of our department, as well as the law officers of the Justice department, found it most difficult to do that. I have had them prepare what I am offering to-day, that is, legislative authority to make agreements, and in all particulars where they will apply the provisions will be similar to those of the Railway Belt Waters Act. That is briefly all I am asking to be dene to-day.
I understand that in one case in Alberta, while they have not in any sense passed a water-powers administration act, they have as a government secured authority from their legislature to take advantage of this legislation when passed by the Dominion parliament. So that the matter will be simply one of agreement between the two governments, this government binding itself to turn over the complete administration of the water-powers of the province.
I may observe in passing, however, that some difficulties are bound to arise in connection with the administration of these powers. In every instance in which a waterpower will be created the streams are interprovincial. This has caused us a good deal of difficulty 'in the province of Manitoba; and

Natural Resources-Western Provinces
without in any way reflecting on any authority I think it is fortunate that the federal government had some control in relation to the administration of water-powers as between Ontario and Manitoba. Some very serious difficulties arose there, and I think I am safe in saying that it was by the good offices of the federal government that these difficulties were ironed out, with the result that they enjoy a complete utilization of the Winnipeg river and of the waters that flow out of Ontario into and through Manitoba. No doubt the same situation will present itself in connection with the administration of the water-powers of the three western provinces, but it is highly probable that the transfer of all these resources will take place in the near future, and the water-powers will, of course, go with all other resources. But from this date on, whenever the provinces are ready to avail themselves of it, they will have complete control of the administration of the water-powers, subject, of course, only to the same provision as is contained in the Railway Belt Water Act, namely, the right of veto on the part of the Minister of the Interior of the federal government.

The natural resources should be turned over to the provinces and although we have had many promises that this would be done we are now asked to pass this particular bill before the fulfilment of those promises. A year ago the Prime Minister himself made the promise that the three western provinces would receive their natural resources after the last session of parliament, but we are still in the same position.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Civil government-immigration and colonization-salary, $314,505; contingencies, $45,000.
I notice that there is an increase in the salary of the deputy minister; would the minister explain the basis of that increase?

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speechtext: It was made by order in council. I suppose the government thought that that was an adequate salary, or at least that the deputy minister was deserving of that increase.
Is the deputy the only one to receive an increase? There have been no increases issued around the House of Commons at all, or is that within the power of the minister?
No.

Item agreed to.
Immigration outside service-salaries, $1,080,000.
Would the minister give us the particulars of the increases which amount to nearly $200,000?

They have amounted to
$330,000 in four years.
How many new employees would be included in that increase?
Thirty-five.
That would not use up the whole $185,000 ; 35 people would hardly average that much.

I rise to protest against
the amount of money that is being spent in the Immigration department. I am not particularly criticizing the minister of the day, but the whole policy for many years past seems to be wrong. I have some figures which I wish to place upon Hansard. Some of them have been given before, but as they are important they are worth repeating. The estimate for the present year is $3,462,900, or an increase of $178,267 over that of a year ago. The census of 1921 shows that Canada had a population of 8,788.000, while the immigrants received in the period from 1921 to 1928 numbered 962,000; the births in Canada from 1921 to 1928 have been 1,939,000, making a total that we should have of 11,689,000 people.
288S
Supply-Immigration

If we deduct from this number the deaths of
824,000	during those years, we should have a balance remaining of 10,805,000. According to the Bureau of Statistics, the estimated population for 1929 is 9,655,000, or a shrinkage in eight years of 1,210,000 people. We have been spending around $3,000,000 a year on immigration and losing at the rate of 1,210 people in eight years, or in other words we have been losing people just about as fast as we have been bringing them in. Furthermore, a number of people who come in do so on their own, and if we charge the whole cost against those people who come in through seeing immigration literature, this would make the figures still worse.
Going back as far as 1881, I find that we have brought in altogether, according to a statement made by the Minister of Immigration as reported in Hansard of March 15, about 5,000,000 people. But we have paid out, according to th| departmental figures, to bring in that number of people, no less a sum than $51,618,024. It seems to me that if all our departments pursued the same policy as the Department of Immigration, where we are paying out a great deal of money and not getting results and where, if we are getting the people, we are not keeping them, this country would be about bankrupt. Furthermore, the great effort for many years has been to place the incoming immigrants on the land, which is about the last place that we should attempt to place them, as long as farming is practically the poorest paying business in this country.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) during the budget debate placed some illuminating figures on Hansard. [DOT]: She showed that in 1926, of insurance funds to the amount of some $73,000,000 invested in farm mortgages, there was in round figures a loss of $1,313,000, while at the same time investments made to the amount of $192,000,000 in urban mortgages, or two and three-quarter times as much, showed a loss of only $256,000, or one-fifth the loss that was made in investments in rural mortgages. It has been shown more than once that every $7 invested in agriculture brings a return of $1. Any man who has been in the game for the last twenty or twenty-five 3'ears knows, taking everything into consideration, that is practically correct. On the other hand, we find that an investment of $3 in industry brings a return of 82.
I want to comment for a moment or two upon some of the propaganda that is being used. A great deal of it is half true, which is far worse than a direct lie. People who do

not know any better are likely to think what is being said is absolutely true and are misled by it. The other day I saw a pamphlet entitled "Boy Settlement in Canada" issued under the authority of the Minister of Immigration, and the following is a quotation from it:
The settled portions of Canada lie in much the same latitude as do the British isles, except that some portions of Canada reach further south than any part of England. Indeed, the southernmost' parts of Canada are further south than any part of France. The seasons in Canada correspond with the seasons in Great Britain, and the practices and customs of the people are practically the same.
That is absolutely correct as far as latitude goes, but climatic conditions in the two countries are entirely different; practices in many ways are also quite different, and the statement is very misleading. I do not think for a moment the Minister of Immigration saw that pamphlet before it went out because I believe enough in his honesty to feel that he would not have allowed it to be issued. This is a further statement from the same pamphlet:
Why should one select farming in Canada as a life pursuit? Because it offers all the advantages which have already been set down as contributing to real success. There is first the prospect of a good financial return from the very beginning.
That in itself is not true. There have been a few fortunate men who have in a short time probably made a good return on their outlay, but the minister knows as well as anybody else in the house that the majority of people who take up farming, either east or west, do not make a fortune and-do not make an easy living in a short time. I should like to quote the following from the speech made by the minister only the other day:
I say that quite a large percentage of those who started with open prairie under very favourable circumstances have failed.
That is quite different from the statements made in this pamphlet issued under his authority. This is another statement that the minister made:
Will the population that is at present living in Canada gain by a tremendously increased immigration?

What is the hon. member
reading from?

I am reading from Hansard a statement made by the minister in the house a few days ago. The minister said further:
But a large immigration does not necessarily mean that we shall be happier or more prosperous.

Supply-Immigration
In that I quite agree with him. Yet he brings in these estimates showing an increase year after year and asks us to pass them without criticism. I should like to refer to another statement that has been issued. I cannot blame the Minister of Immigration in this case, but I picked up a pamphlet issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; a quotation from which is as follows in reference to last year's crop:
Not only has the generality of crop production been uniformly fine and satisfactory but many yields have been recorded which would in other countries be considered exceptional or beyond possibility but to which western Canada in her bumper years has grown accustomed.
There is a misleading statement. It goes on:
Yields between 50 and 60 bushels to the acre have been fairly common-
That is referring to last year's crop:
-and there have been many in excess of this, ranging as high as 88 bushels per acre, which, for the extent over which production was secured, is considered a world record.
Nothing could be more misleading. I cannot blame the minister or his department in a case like this, but at the same time I think it is his duty or the duty of his officials to contradict such extraordinarily foolish and irrational statements that are going out supposedly on accepted authority. We all know that there was great promise of a fairly good crop last year, but we also know that owing to a disastrous frost before the crop ripened, the yield was cut down easily one-third and much more in some cases, and the average yield in the province from which I come was 18 bushels per acre instead of reaching to 50 or 60 or 88 bushels per acre.
Not only are we spending this large amount directly under the Department of Immigration, $3,462,000, but under the land settlement board, according to the estimates, we are also spending $1,400,000, and under the Department of Health, we are spending on immigration, $300,000 and I understand that the railways have also paid approximately $1,500,000 to bring in immigrants, or a total of $6,662,000. At the same time, with all this expenditure, we are not increasing our population. It does seem to me that we-would be ahead in this country if we closed down for the time being our Immigration department. The work could easily be looked after by, say, the Minister of Agriculture, who would know where agriculturists were needed. The Minister of Labour would also be in a good position to say when more labour was needed in Canada, and probably the work of the Minister of National Health could be increased a little because he has already considerable work to do in connection with immigration. It does seem to me that we are spending a lot of good public money uselessly through this department. I am not going to criticize the minister because I think probably he is doing his work as well as any other minister who has filled that position, but the whole immigration policy of this country for the last twenty years or so has been wrong. Since 1881 we have spent over $51,000,000 and brought in 5,000,000 people, most of whom we have lost. I think that fact proves my contention.	-
Further, such schemes as are being put forward for forcing more people into this country, and putting them on the land to grow greater quantities of wheat, is another proof that the policy we are following is along false lines. It is only this year that having only two-thirds of the crop we expected last year, with the world's crop being somewhat large, prices have dropped lower than we have had for several years. What would prices have been if our crop had developed as we hoped it would in 1928?
Then we have people-I am glad to know they are not farmers, and they will not be farmers, because they see too clearly the direction in which we are drifting-but people who are not farmers who eventually hope to .take advantage of those who are on the land are advocating different immigration schemes from time to time. The minister knows perfectly well that it is a false line of argument to say that we need more people in this country and particularly on the land. What we should aim at is to improve conditions so that there will be a decent standard of living on the farms, and when the man on the land is assured of a reasonable return on his capital outlay and from the labour he expends, then we need not be afraid of not getting enough people into this country; because the job then will be to keep them out. But to-diay when those engaged in the basic industry of this country are not enjoying a decent standard of living, and the minister knows perfectly well that they are not-the standard of living of the farmer from the east to the west is not nearly so 'high as it ought to be considering the amount of capital he invests and the amount of energy he puts into his work-we are going out to seek immigrants, but until we get a decent standard of living for the man on the land, is it worth while to spend any more public money trying to get immigrants to come to this country to farm?
There is one other point. Other hon. members have asked for figures showing how many
Supply-Immigration

Canadians have left this country, but we are always given the reply: "0'h, the figure cannot be Stated. The cost of gathering that data is too much, so we have not kept a record." I would ask why cannot the same officials who check the people coming into the country also check the people going out. Then we would know where we stood. At the present time we have to go to the officials at Washington to find out how many people have left this country for the United States. Surely with all the money that is being spent on this department we Should have an accurate statement of who is coming into this country, who they are, what they do, and how many leave. I do think that we are making a tremendous mistake spending a huge sum of money every year on immigration, When we are not doing any more than just keeping our population at its present level.

I might make some explanation of the increase in this vote as compared with last year. The vote this year is $1,080,000; last year it was $1,033,955, but owing to a mistake of the accountant that amount was not included in the estimates last year, and so we asked for a supplementary estimate of $138,955 last year, which we did not get. The Minister of Finance told us that we had better try and get through with what we had, and we had to do so. We were accordingly unable to create the organization that we had in mind last year, and we had to carry quite a number of employees as temporaries who should 'have been on the permanent list. The temporary list will be smaller this year owing to a number of the temporaries 'being put on the permanent list.

What was the amount
expended last year?
Mr. FORIiE : We got along with less than the amount asked for. In reality there is not much difference between the vote this year and last. I cannot say just how much the expenditure for temporary help was increased owing to our not having the amount in the estimates last year.
Mr. CH'APLIN:	Surely the minister can
tell us exactly what was expended last year independent of whether these men were temporary or permanent employees.

The actual amount spent
was $863,841. I should perhaps make an explanation right here. Although this estimate calls for a certain amount of money it does not follow that that amount has been spent. I think I will be able to show that before I am through.
If the minister spent only $895,000 last year why is he asking for $1,080,000 this year? It is over $200,000 more.

My deputy informs me that
the reorganization, that was intended last year did not go into effect, and the amount of money that we intended to spend last year was not spent.

Will the minister explain
the reorganization he refers to?

Well it extends all through
the service, putting it on a more efficient basis. We may not be getting very many immigrants but we are getting sufficient to require a very efficient service.

Does the minister mean
that the whole service is to be reorganized, every branch of it?

It has been reorganized.
The reorganization is complete.

And it will cost $200,000
more to handle it.
I suppose it will.
What proportion of this vote is purely for the purpose of securing immigrants?

That more properly belongs to the next vote. I think I can give you the details. This is the cost of the permanent outside service.

Mr. Chairman, I notice
in the Auditor General's report that there is given a list of places where the minister has agencies, presumably for the purpose of getting immigrants. Will the minister tell us how many immigrants he gets, for instance, from San Francisco, where he has an agency, or is this just a place where some good Canadian can go for a rvinter holiday? I am surprised that I do not see in this list such places as San Diego and Florida, although I notice an agency at Manchester, New Hampshire, which is in the Green mountains, or the White

Supply-Immigration
mountains. I suppose that is a good place for a summer resort but not much of a place to get immigrants. Will the minister explain the necessity for an office at San Francisco or Spokane?

I had better read down the
whole list.
Just give us San Francisco for example.

There were 132 inquiries,
426 interviews, prospects of 35 farmers, and [DOT] others who called were 12. Forty-seven heads of families came to Canada, 93 people all told, and they brought in from San Francisco last year capital to the amount of $163,240.
What was the cost of the office at that point?
The cost of that office was $13,000 according to the Auditor General's report.
Does that include the oil prospectors and operators?

My deputy handed me the wrong paper. I was rather surprised myself at the numbers that I had to read out. The number of inquiries last year at San Francisco was 1,593; heads of families, 188; number of immigrants, 463; number of carloads of settlers' effects, 2; value of effects, $402,120; good prospects outstanding, 47.
Do I understand that the value of two carloads was $462,120?
That is what it says here.
Well you had better have those figures revised. Would the minister just explain that $402,120, the value of two carloads of settlers' effects?
That is the total brought into the country. They 'brought in two carloads, and the total effects included cash and everything else amounting to $402,120.
Where is the office from which we had 47 families?
That was for the same place, but it was only a monthly report.
Has the minister any information as to what pursuits those families engaged in when they came to Canada? Were they farmers?
I think they were all farmers. I have not the report here. Farmers are the only clas that we are recruiting over there.
There is no recruiting going on for any other class except farmers as far as that office is concerned
No.
Will the minister kindly answer the question I put to him? Why cannot we check up the people going from Canada to the States?
I am mot an expert at that. My deputy informs me that to do that would take about double the organization we have.
Is that because there are so many leaving?

With regard to the figures we get from the Bureau of Statistics at Washington, I believe they probably overstate the number of people who really leave Canada. The other day I looked over some statistics of the number of people in the United States born in Canada; the number is growing less every ten years, so that if the volume of emigration to the United States was as great as it is claimed to be, the number of native born Canadians in the United States would be on the increase.

But a large proportion
of those going over from Canada are not native born Canadians. They are people who are naturalized Canadians, and they usually put themselves down as English, Irish, Scotch, French, or whatever nationality they belong to, so that they are not entered as Canadians at all. Now frequently the minister and his officials make precisely the same statement which the minister has just made, namely, that these figures are all wrong which we obtain from the American offices in regard to Canadians going to the United States. On what ground do they make the statement? Surely the United States authorities have no reason for padding their immigration list to show a larger proportion of Canadians entering that country than actually do go in. Indeed, there is far less reason for the United States to pad their immigration figures than there is for the Minister of Immigration here to pad his. Are we therefore to draw the conclusion that the minister is judging the United States immigration department by his own? Are we to conclude that the Canadian figures are wrong and that they are being padded? Unless the minister can prove to us that the American figures are wrong I see no reason why he should question them. We do not keep any record ourselves of Canadians leaving this country, so that the only means we have of finding out is to take the figures given
Supply-Immigration

by the officials of the United States immigration department. And those figures, we are always being told, are wrong. I repeat, unless the minister can prove that they are wrong it is time the government stopped challenging them. I personally have no reason for believing that those figures are wrong. On my desk I have the figures for the past ten years and I can tell the minister that a large proportion of Canadians leaving this country are not native born but naturalized.
I do not like to exaggerate the number of people leaving Canada for the United States.
We are not exaggerating; we are giving the official figures.
Instead of making the number larger I should prefer to make it as small as I could.
We find that other ministers take the same view.

Hon. members know that
the statistics for past years will show that the condition was much worse years ago than it is now.

Never. The worst years
we have had have been the past six or seven under this government, and I make that statement without fear of contradiction by anyone. There is no doubt whatever that, according to the figures supplied by the United States, the worst years we have had were those particularly from 1923 to 1927. The last two years have not been quite so bad, but generally speaking the last six or seven have been the worst period we have ever had of emigration to the United States. There is not an atom of doubt about that. I shall be glad to be corrected if I am wrong, but I do not think I can be corrected because I have checked the figures. I resent the implication that we wish to paint things worse than they are; we paint them simply in accordance with the official figures of the United States. I want to tell the minister that we are just as optimistic as he is in regard to this great country; in fact, we are more so, because the other day he uttered a wail of despair about Canada. He took the same attitude as has been taken this morning by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer). We have a country containing immense areas, magnificent resources and vast possibilities, a country with a greater future than that of any other country in the world. To my mind there is not the slightest doubt about that; yet the minrMr. Manion.]
ister and the hon. member for Battle River throw up their hands and say, "We do not want immigrants to come to Canada." Are we going to put up our shutters and bar our doors and windows against prospective Canadians?

Let people come in
naturally; don't force them.

Every country that wants immigration must take the proper means to see that it gets the right type of immigrant, and to this end there must be some . organization. I do not agree for a moment with the hon. member in this regard. I do n-ot dispute the suggestion that there may be too much money spent on immigration for the results we are getting; I am not sure that this is not correct. But I do not see how you can possibly handle immigration without an adequate organization, and certainly I cannot endorse any such idea as that this magnificent country should put up its shutters and close its doors completely, taking the stand,
" We have great resources; let us hang on to them and keep other people out." Surely we have a more encouraging conception of Canada's future greatness. I personally do not understand the attitude taken by the hon. member for Battle River and by the minister himself.

It is rather unfortunate that I should be attacked by the hon. member for Battle River and then by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) for entirely different reasons. One complains that I am admitting too many immigrants and the other suggests that I do not admit any. I see that the Toronto Globe makes the statement that I am like Daniel in the lions' den.

And just as helpless, I
am afraid.

Let us hope the Lord is
with me anyhow.

The lions roar but they
don't bite.

I take second place to no
hon. member in my faith in this Dominion, and I do not like to hear the hon. member for Battle River speaking about excessively hard times. According to the speeches heard in 1921 and 1922, there was nothing but ruin and degradation and misery facing us at that time.

Was that not correct
at that time?

Supply-Immigration

But we are all here and
just as well off.

The minister was better
off then.
The minister was one of those who were wailing then.
The item under discussion is an important one; will the minister give the headings of expenditure. What, for instance, is the expense in connection with advertising?

This item is entirely for
salaries; I can read over the list if my hon. friend wishes.
No, I do not want the individual salaries. I thought there were some other items besides salaries.
No, this is entirely salaries.

It seems to me that for
a department which is showing as little result as the Immigration department the least we can do is to keep salaries where they were before. I do not see any excuse whatever for increasing salaries in this department. If we are getting somewhere there might be some excuse, but this is a hopeless proposition; it is absolutely impossible; you are wasting money.

Since the minister has
gone over to the other side he has lost touch with agriculture in this country. He knows perfectly well that agriculture has been in trouble for many' years, and the hon. member for Fort William will realize this too if only he will look into the matter closely.

We have feiw of the
troubles which my hon. friend deplores so much.

We are spending $51,-
000,000 and bringing in 5,000,000 people and losing them. Is that good business? I think it is bad business.

We do not spend $51,000,-
000.

I am taking your own
figures.

I have been discussing immigration estimates for the last ten or twelve years and I am further behind now than when I started. I am not impressed with the policy of the government; I never was; I have always criticized them and I think rightly so.
But never voted.

There never was a vote
on these immigration estimates in the house.
No? Well, let us have one now. I will support any resolution you propose for reducing this estimate.
What good will that do?
It will save a lot of money anyway.

As a matter of fact, I am
in favour of spending much more than we spend now. I am in favour of the open door; I want to bring into the country everyone who wants to come and who is white, healthy and mentally and morally fit. That is the party to which I belong and I am sorry to say I have not one follower yet.
What about the Minister of Finance?

I do not know what his
views are on this point; he is so busy with finance that he cannot bother with immigration.
Why not move a resolution with regard to this one-man party you talk about?

Who will second it? I
merely rose to answer the statement made by the hon. member for Fort William. He speaks about the overwhelming exodus from this country, particularly in the years 192425. He should know that was due entirely to the quota law of the United States; in 1924 they put into force a very drastic quota law which made it imperative for them to allow Canadians into their country if they were to have any immigration at all. Under the two per cent quota only some 100,000 or
150,000	people from Europe are allowed to enter the United States, but all native born Canadians can go into the United States without let or hindrance, and I should say they are rather a good element to have; they are as good as any immigrants the United States could get and they are equal to any of the people residing in that country now, so it is not at all surprising that they put into force this rule which prevents unrestricted immigration from Europe. This is the only country from which they can draw immigrants.

Mexico is on the same
basis.

The trouble with us is
that the whole of Europe is going into the United States through Canada.

My hon. friend should know that is not what is happening.
Supply-Immigration
I do know; I am on the border as much as you are, and that is what is happening.

I think my hon. friend is on the border of unreason when he makes that statement; we have here the figures showing the number of people who enter Canada. My hon. friend should know how difficult it is for people to come to this country; the rules are being applied in a most drastic manner, because it as the wish of this parliament. It seems to me that the Minister of Immigration should have some support here. We have the hon. member for Fort William on the one hand and the hon. member for Battle River on the other advising different courses; those behind cry "forward" and those in front cry "back", so what is the minister to do? He cannot take the advice of both.
He can stand still, as he is doing now.	*

No, I did not advocate
bringing in sheep; I advocated building up the sheep population by a proper policy.

Yes, bringing in men and
bringing up sheep.
You want to bring in the goats.

No, I want to send the goats back if they turn out to be goats. Up to the present there never has been any difficulty in absorbing immigrants in this country. I venture to say that in the great city of Montreal, which has a population of about
1,250,000,	there are not 500 people unemployed, and those people could obtain employment if they went after it. That condition exists in every city throughout Canada, and there is no reason why that should not be so. This country is just on the eve of an immense expansion; we read every day about the mines in the north, the lumbering, the pulp and paper industry and so on, but only certain classes of people will do the menial work connected with these industries. Tb use the expression of my hon. friend from Fort William, you cannot get red-blooded Canadians to do work that Italians, Czechoslovakians and others will do. They will not do it; Canadians have gone up in the social scale and the digging of canals, the building of railways and all that sort of work must be done by the foreigner. In the second generation the foreigner's children will not do that work either; they will want to become members of parliament, university professors and so on, and that is only right. This is a country for ambitious people; it is a country of ambition.
Under our immigration regulations the map of Europe is divided according to racial lines; for instance, an Austrian cannot come to Canada unless the minister permits him to enter, while on the other hand a German has no trouble coming here. It would take a person more clever than many hon. members of this house, including myself, to tell the difference between an Austrian and a German. Why should Austrians be kept out and Germans permitted to enter? I cannot see. any reason.

I will tell the hon. gentleman one reason. As a matter of experience one finds that frequently the German is the man who owns, controls or directs a business, whereas the Austrian gravitates towards that lower class of labour to which my hon. friend has referred. That is a very marked difference between the two.
I do not see why a barber who comes from Berlin is a better man than a 'barber who comes from Vienna.

Thait is not the proper comparison.

Supply-Immigration

Yes, it is; they do not make any distinction between Germans and Austrians in that respect. Then we will not admit Italians. I am not here for the purpose of eulogizing the Italians or any other people, but accepting the theory laid down by the Immigration department, I claim an Italian from the north of Italy is quite as good as a German from central Germany; there is no difference. Why should a man from Italian Lomlbardy be refused entrance to Canada while a German from Berlin or Frankfort is permitted to enter?
We get Italian immigrants now.

We are not getting very
many of them.
Mussolini will not let them out; he needs them all at home.
That is a good reason why my hon. friend will not let them in; he is in alliance with Mussolini.
They are dodging Montreal, that is all.

We have room for Italians
in Montreal, and we have room for other people from Europe; we have been taking them for 150 years and so has the United States. I say it is silly on the part of this country, which is looking for population according to my hon. friend from Fort William, to refuse admittance to these people.

Will my hon.
friend say that no Italians enter Canada?

Italian agriculturists are
allowed in, but that is all.

That applies to
other countries too.

That applies to every other country in Europe. Take Russia, a country with 140,000.000 people of stern, hardy stock; I think every one will admit that these are people who should be welcomed to Canada, because they know what work really is. They have been living close to the ground, and that is the class of people we want in a country like this, which is just beginning its expansion and development. The most noticeable thing in the whole affair is the fact that everyone else seems to know something about the matter except those who should be primarily interested, namely the Canadian Ukrainians. It thus becomes very evident that some unknown person who has an axe to grind wishes to further his interests at the expense of the Ukrainians. This can be inferred from the extreme haste with which this false rumour was so widely propagated; it can be detected in the awkward manner in which two contradictory lines of action are contemplated, including as it does in this fantastic manoeuvre the Hungarians and Czechoslovaks, and finally concluding with a foolhardy political threat.
We believe that the new immigration restrictions will not hurt the Ukrainians very much since they will, notwithstanding, still be able to bring in their relatives and friends to Canada on affidavits or special permits; and that only those central European nationalities would be affected which had none of their own farmers in Canada.
Notwithstanding this, however, we understand that, certain interested factors are furthering their efforts in the same direction with a view to finding real facts to prove their untenable theory. It is therefore, quite possible that some group of impostors, posing as "representatives of the Ukrainian population", for certain considerations will allow itself to be utilized in the above-mentioned scheme, even going so far as to actually rallying our citizens in western Canada with a view to deluging Ottawa with petitions in the interests of the Ukrainian people.
We therefore most decisively wish to note that this whole affair is the initiative of some non-Ukrainian body; that nobody has the right in such an irresponsible manner to abuse the good name of the Canadian Ukrainians. The new immigration restriction with respect to farm labourers from central Europe will do us little harm if our farmers make an early effort to secure permits for their relatives and friends and thus give them an opportunity to arrive here early in the spring.

What occurs is this: a native Canadian coming back to Canada from the United States for the summer, or to visit relatives, is asked when he gets to the port of entry, "How long have you been cut of Canada?" Last year there was before the committee a motion which I regret that the minister dlid not include among the recommendations. We have had suggestions from various sections of the house regarding the manner in which the Department of Immigration has fallen down in not bringing more farmers in. It seems to me a logical question to ask-what is the matter with the Canadian fanner? If we look up the statistics we shall find that the Canadian farmer to-day is making more progress than the farmer of any other country the wide world over. For instance, at this very moment the United States congress is holding a special session for the purpose of introducing measures for the relief of American farmers. No one has ever heard of this parliament doing any such thing for the Canadian farmer. In the British Empire the farmers have been relieved of practically all taxes. Nothing of the sort has been done fqr our farmers. On the other hand, the per capita production of the Canadian farmer is greater than that of the farmer of any other country in the world. So that I believe we have in Canada probably the most competent aggregation of farmers to be found anywhere in the world. I would ask, therefore: What do you expect to do by bringing in from other countries a lot of farmers who are not so competent as the farmers at present in Canada? Take the price of grain to-day, which is lower than it has been at any time in the past fifteen years. Certainly it would be economically unsound to bring in a lot more farmers and have them grow more grain without making provision for an additional market. Dairy production in Canada has been very rapidly falling off in the last th-ree 'years and will depreciate still further. On the other hand, the Canadian fanners are helping to support the agricultural implement manufacturers, who charge a good deal more for their implements than do the manufacturers of any other country. So that the Canadian farmer has reached the distinctive position where he *can get along without government assistance and even in spite of the handicap in regard to the purchase of implements.

If we should come to a period of extreme depression, which undoubtedly is coming in the agricultural industry, and these fellows get a little behind with their payments, consider the difference between their situation and that of the man who is dealing directly with the implement agent. Then we must consider the question of markets and the further question of special privileges which are granted to our immigrants but are not granted to our established farmers. The proposals which are being considered in the United States at the moment undoubtedly will hurt the western farmer. If a farmer in western Canada has made good', if he thinks that his brother coming out can also make good, and if he is pre-
pared to find employment for him, then I say that that is the best kind of immigration policy we can have, and the immigration policy as far as publicity is concerned that we have always advocated. But when the hon. the minister speaks of 600 labourers, that perhaps brings up a slightly different point. If those 600 were individual applications from men who themselves were prepared to offer employment then all right, but dif it was simply an estimate placed upon the potential needs of a district by people who perhaps are not qualified to have an opinion, then it is a very different question altogether. . I am fairly familiar with the workings of the department, because I have tried to follow the work in its different branches, not in an antagonistic spirit hut in order to work with them if I can for the betterment of conditions here. And in doing that I found myself up against that very thing the minister has spoken of; the intimation to the department by individuals, or groups of individuals, that there will be certain mass vacancies, and that certain districts can absorb so many hundreds, or bo many thousands of farm help, which is a very different thing from personal nominations, and while I approve of the one I am far from approving of the other.
Just one more point in that particular connection; I have indicated our attitude, or my conception at least of cur attitude, towards the subject of immigration itself. And I have indicated that we are not opposed to immigration as such, but we are only opposed to what is commonly called assisted or encouraged immigration, that is over-encouraged. We are willing to have people come in if they are decent people, but we are not so far gone in Canada that we must give approval to the idea qf going out into the highways and byways morally compelling people to come. We are particularly opposed to that because those who are compelled to come are almost invariably people of our own class whom we will have to assimilate, and our condition will be adversely or beneficially affected by them. Again I say that if any in Canada have a right to speok on immigration it is those who will have to shoulder the burden of immigration, the burden of assimilation, and to whom assimilation is not a mere sounding phrase but a natural matter of everyday life in connection with neighbours for whom they have had no responsibility and in the selection of whom they have had no choice.
That brings me to the next point. I read with a great deal of interest, and followed

Supply-Immigration
very carefully the discussion in the agriculture committee of last year, and I studied, so far as I could study, the recommendations. The recommendation there which struck me as being the soundest and the most sensible, and offering the greatest potentialities for future success in our work was that simple suggestion that to the provinces themselves should be delegated a greater pant of the responsibility, a greater part of the authority as to how many and what classes should come into those provinces.
But how can you get them to take it? They do not like to.

Possibly they do not like to, but I a.m inclined to think, from such knowledge as I possess of the views of one at least of the provincial governments, that if given that right and given it without strings-given that right so that they would be not merely expressing an opinion but taking action1-they would undertake it. And more than that, I believe it is the only method whereby you will properly provide for immigration; for, after all, once the immigrant crosses the portals of this country he ceases to be a responsibility of the government who brought him out and becomes a direct responsibility of the province, who have had no say as to whether or not he should be here. And that to my mind is wrong.
Working with our municipal authorities, discussing the matter with our own government, I have found this. We have the very finest machinery in the world for ascertaining how many people can be properly and profitably absorbed in a province during the year. We have information on which a competent committee decide as to where people may properly go, as to the kind of people who are desired, as to the occupation which will afford them opportunities. Through all the various municipal councils in the provinces the authorities can supply, and I am sure, from applications to myself, that they would be willing to supply, full Statistics as to any possible vacant farm which may lie within their boundaries, as to the amount of capital that would be necessary to enable a farmer to go on that farm, as to the kind of people they would like to have in the district-and this depends partly on the class of people already settled there. They could furnish the government with that information, and I am sure they would.
I have a suggestion to offer, and I do not claim that it is particularly a constructive one or particularly a new one. However, let that suggestion come from whichever side it may,
it should be tried out partly from time to time-and in this lies our only hope of mastering the problem of increased population. My suggestion is this: The provincial government, through municipal machinery, know what employment is in sight for the year; they know what lands are available; they know what the effect of increased population on the farming industry generally will be in the province; and they might make a reasonably intelligent report. On that report the Department of Immigration here could act through its agent, admitting any desired number of immigrants, seeing that their destination was wise, advising them as to the parts of the country to which they might go, giving them all information possible as to the means of reaching their destination, and supplying them with information as to the best way in which to carry on after they had arrived. There is a great work for the Immigration department to do in the elimination of the unfit and in giving information and advice to those people who come to the country, often bewildered and ignorant of our halbits and sometimes of our language. The department could do a splendid work in that way. And it should give to the provinces some at least of the authority which should go with the responsibility that becomes theirs the moment an immigrant enters Canada.
My time is almost up, but I was asked a question which I shall try to answer. The question is: Why are so many people leaving the farms? In the first place, it is undoubtedly a question of dollars and cents; that is what Strikes one primarily in looking into the matter. Is farming a congenial business, is it a profitable business? Well, the minister knows that while it is one of the finest forms of life-and I believe this because I have followed it all my life-farming is a life that imposes upon the man who pursues it a great many hardships. He has to face hard physical labour; he has to work out in the snow and rain and cold winds; he has to take a sporting chance as a gambler with nature, as to whether or not he will have any results at all from his year's toil. He has to face all these conditions; he has to work hours longer by far than those which are put in in any other industry, except possibly in this house; he has to work under conditions more uncertain than those that prevail in any other occupation; and frequently he has to work in loneliness and deprivation so far as social comfort is concerned. And when you add to all this the fact that no farmer- no farmer, at least, of whom I have knowledge
Supply-Immigration

-ever made more than a decent living, while many farmers, to <my knowledge, in spite of honest and earnest effort have failed and gone down, you can see the reason why farmers leave.
But there is another reason and perhaps it is more fundamental still. To my mind it does not make very much difference in the long run how profitable farming is; you are bound to have an exodus from the country to the cities, and for this reason. During my lifetime in that province-and I am still a comparatively young man-the productive ability of every man has increased four or five times through the introduction and use of labour-saving units of machinery. The result is that it is requiring a smaller and smaller percentage of men to produce the necessary amount of food. While that does not apply absolutely to all Canada-because we feed other countries than our own-it undoubtedly does apply to agriculture as a whole, and there is no question that it must and will apply to Canada generally as time goes on. A smaller and smaller percentage of men will remain on the land and a larger percentage will go to the centres, because in these centres are new industries providing for all the new wants, and luxuries which, deplored by some, are in my opinion a dispensation of Providence in that they absorb the labour continually thrown off from the basic industries by the adoption of larger and larger units of machinery. Throughout the world, therefore, and in this country as well- for Canada is not immune from the law of supply and demand-no matter how profitable farming may be, no matter how agreeable the conditions may be made, no matter how hard men may work, it will happen inevitably that a larger percentage of men will be found in the cities and a smaller percentage on the' land. But while that is true it does not mean that we should add thereto the factors of economic uncertainty and lack of economic reward.
I must apologize for having spoken at greater length than I had intended, I got up in the first place simply to correct a misapprehension with reference to our attitude towards immigration, and I did not expect to be led into so long a discourse as I have made. My chief interest at the moment is to direct the attention of the committee to the question of land settlement, a question regarding which I have some knowledge, with which I have been fairly closely in touch, and on which I hold some fairly strong opinions. However, I shall leave that until the proper item comes up. In the meantime, I repeat for emphasis -because apparently it is an exceedingly

difficult thing for other people sometimes to appreciate the fact-that we are not opposed to people coming into the country but that we are opposed, for the credit and for the economic future of Canada, to the idea of going out and inducing or assisting them to come here.

Some of the remarks that
have been made lead me to believe that this is an opportune moment to make a statement as to the actual cost to Canada of immigration. We have heard the figure of five millions stated, and I have seen six and a half millions reported as having been suggested in a public speech not very long ago. I have the figures for last year and I will give them. The cost of securing immigrants for Canada was $1,404,463.30; that is the actual cost of our immigration offices and the seeking and securing of immigrants. The care and placement of these immigrants after landing in Canada was $196,294.12. This makes a total, for recruiting immigrants and taking care of them after arrival in Canada, of $1,600,757.42.
Does that include everything?
That is the cost of bringing them to Canada and looking after them.

In what way do you
take care of them?
Well, getting the immigrant a situation, if he is farm help, or getting him placed if he is a farmer.

There were some immigrants who came to Alberta for whom the province had no responsibility but who were brought out by the minister's department. They were stranded in Calgary and we had to take care of them. Hospital bills were incurred amounting to some $1,000 towards which we asked the department to contribute, but they washed their hands entirely of responsibility in the matter. Will some of the money to which the minister has just referred be used to take care of these immigrants? Will his department pay that bill?

I do not know who those
immigrants were:

minister has given include cost of civil government?

No, they do not include
civil government.

Is not that part of the
cost of immigration?

Then there is another thing which the house may have forgotten. During the last few years and particularly during the last year the United States made a great clean up, I think every crook in that country has headed towards Canada lately, and if we had not possessed a good preventive service we would have had a large increase in our population made up of that kind of people. Some people cannot understand why there should be any immigration inspectors at all, but not a day passes without some undesirable characters being turned back at the border. Then there is the administrative service, amounting to $480,165.36, making the total estimate for last year of $2,865,685.44. In order to obtain the total amount spent by the department there must be added $600,000 which was charged up to the land settlement branch under the Soldier Settlement Board, and that will give a total of about $3,400,000 as the actual amount spent last year. I do not know where my hon. friends secured the figure of $6,000,000; I cannot see where that came from at all.

inspection also?

No, the medical inspection
accounts for another $300,000, but that would have to go on even if there were no immigration. We might have a smaller staff, but _ we would still have medical inspection.

be the medical inspection overseas, which would account for another $300,000, and that would bring the total to nearly $4,000,000.
Probably that would be correct.

when the total as shown by the Auditor General's report, page 836, is only $3,065,000.

I should like to follow
up the question I was asking a few moments ago, with regard to the immigrants being required to state what religion they profess. The minister suggested an amendment to the regulation so that the immigrants would not need to give so many details, but then he said this information was useful both for the census bureau and for the churches, which were glad to get it. First I would like to ask the minister if this information is passed on to the churches?
If they ask for it.

Whether they ask for
it or not I know that representatives of the churches usually meet the immigrants at the port of debarkation and ask them personally as to their religion. I passed through the immigration sheds at Quebec in 1927 for the purpose of seeing how this was done. I found different ministers asking the immigrants personally to what churches they belonged, so I think it is quite unnecesary to ask that question if it is done only for the purpose of supplying information to the churches. As far as the census goes, we get all the information we need from the census statistics, so I think we would be well advised not to ask that question at all. I take it for granted that no one of good character will be refused entry because of his religion, so I do not see why the question should be asked at all.
These facts are all recorded in the index book on board ship before the immigrant land's. All the religious societies have agents at Quebec, and some at Montreal.

So there is no escape
at all.

I think they do very good
work there. The representatives of the churches are given an opportunity to look at the index book, and they look after people of their own denomination when they land. They get in touch with the friends of the immigrants, tell them they have landed and when they will arrive at their destination, and taken altogether I think a useful purpose is served. There is no publicity; this in-
Supply-Immigration

formation is never published but is simply-obtained for those people who are anxious to get these figures. As I said before, I do not think anyone would be turned back if he simply said he was an agnostic, with no religion at all, so long as his moral character was all right.

But does the minister
realize that many people object to being cross-examined in that way?

What is
objectionable about it?	[DOT]
The hon. member who just interrupted may not object, but certain people of whom I have knowledge do object.

As a matter of information we - think the benefit outweighs any objection which might be taken to it, and the statistical bureau gets that information also. This is not done in order to annoy or restrain these immigrants; it is largely for the benefit of the different religious denominations who like to get that information and really, from my own experience during the last three years, an immigrant is much better off if he is looked after by a religious society, regardless of what denomination he belongs to.

In these figures there are
certain amounts set aside for the repatriation of Canadians.
It is not in the vote.

I have the Auditor General's report, and on page 23 of part H, under "colonization," I find a sum amounting to about $35,000. Under that there appear salaries and wages, $9,204.19 and travelling expenses $25,081.61. In the first instance, the salaries were paid to fourteen clergymen and the travelling expenses were paid to eighteen clergymen. This question was up in the house some time ago and we were advised by the minister that this was for the purpose of repatriating Canadians.

What year is the hon.
member quoting from?
1927-28. Are those clergymen still employed by the government?
No.
What has been substituted for that service?

We have been cooperating
with the provinces and have offered to pay 50 per cent of any amount expended on repatriation. The only province which is actively engaged in this work is the province
fMr. Forke.]
of Quebec, but one of the maritime provinces is thinking of taking up the work. The same offer stands open to every province of the Dominion.

What was the amount
expended last year?

We set aside $50,000 as
the maximum for any one province.
Was that expended?

My deputy informs me
that we expended $29,680 last year.
In one province?

And the province of Quebec spent $46,000, so apparently part of their expenditure must have been in colonization work. I discussed this matter first with Premier Taschereau when he was here a year ago last summer, and then the Minister of Mines and Forests came here and we entered into that bargain. I could not see my way clear to do anything for the province of Quebec which would not be open to all the other provinces. I expect that one of the maritime provinces will go into repatriation work in a short time in an endeavour to bring back some of their people from the New England states. I think the money is well spent, probably bringing in the best results of any money we spend upon immigration.

In connection with this question of repatriation, I would like to read a letter which I received from New Bedford, as follows:
I have just read your speech in the House of Commons on immigration in Canada. I was specially interested in that part of your speech in which you refer to the French' Canadians of New England. Let me tell you that if the government of Ottawa would only lend to a family, say, $1,000 you would have a train going to the Peace River every two weeks of good farmers of Canadian stock who wish to go back to their country and make a home once more on the farm. The Quebec government offers us money to go to the Abitibi district. We don't want to go there, we want to go to the west. We are starving in here and our government does not want to help us get to our mother country. I know quite a number of my friends who wrote to the government in Ottawa asking them for help to go back and every time the answer was "We have no right to do so."
Believe me,
Yours truly,
J. Vachon.
Where is that from?

New Bedford.

Mr. FORIvE: A French Canadian who has been residing in the States for a number of years and who wishes to return to Canada is granted the same rates on the. railroads as an immigrant from Great Britain.

Why not better rates?
Mr. FORIvE:	He gets the immigration
rates. It is the railways which grant those rates. The hardship arises through the fact that a French Canadian who has remained' in his own province has to pay the full rate when he desires to go to the west, while the French Canadian who has gone to the States and wishes to return is granted the cheaper rate.

We were told earlier in the session that the government would not continue to extend aid for highway development or for technical education upon the ground that it was a vicious principle for the federal authorities to subsidize the provinces. I would like to ask upon what principle the government is now subsidizing the provinces in order that they may oarry on this immigration scheme?

I do not think it is in the
nature of a subsidy. They have settled some twelve or thirteen new parishes in the province of Quebec, and' I think the money is well spent.

I am not suggesting that the money is not well spent, but I do suggest that the principle is one which was called a vicious principle earlier in the session and I am anxious to know how it is being justified in this case.

Mr. Chairman, in discussing this immigration question I shall deal with it almost entirely as it concerns the population, colonization and settlement conditions in my own province of New Brunswick. As you are aware, that
province, like the other maritime provinces, has suffered from the migration of its people to the United States and to the six western provinces.
In 1901 we had a population of 321,120; in 1911 this had increased to 351,880, and in 1921 it had increased to 387,876. It might be well to note at this point that the province of New Brunswick has an area of 27,895 square miles. As the greatest migration was from 1921 to 1928, it is doubtful if there has been any increase in population during those years. While the other provinces suffered a loss of population by migration to the United States during that period, New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces suffered an additional drain by migration to the west and to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. While we regret the conditions which forced our people to leave their homes, that regret is tempered, to some degree, by the fact that many of them remained Canadians by locating in other provinces. There is not this feeling towards the other migration as the New Brunswickers who have gone to the United States are lost not only to Neiw Brunswick but to Canada. It is quite possible that in the New England states and the six Canadian provinces west of the maritimes the New Brunswickers and their descendants outnumber those who remain in their native province. This is not as it Should be. New Brunswick is a province of varied and valuable resources. Sixty per cent of it is valuable mixed farming land; there are great pulp and timber resources, valuable water-powers, never-failing fisheries, excellent transportation, and its products are at the Canadian outport for the European trade.
Through St. John many European and British immigrants enter Canada, but the only ones who remain in New Brunswick are those specially selected and brought there by the local government. Do not think that I, as a New Brunswicker-and I believe I represent the prevailing sentiment in that province-am jealous of the expansion in population, wealth and development of Ontario, Quebec and the west. We do not ask the government to relax its work in colonization and settlement in those provinces; in. fact, we urge even greater efforts in their behalf. We welcome Canadian development in every part, but we do ask greater consideration, greater activity, better results in retaining ou.r own people, repatriating those who have gone to the United States, and more satisfactory efforts in adding to our population from the people of Great Britain and Europe, who

Under the heading of "Great Britain and the continent of Europe, Miscellaneous," I find an item of some $8,000 spent for the packing and distributing of Canadian peonies. What was the object of sending those Canadian peonies overseas?
That was in 1927.
I think I may ask for an explanation of this item even if the expenditure took place in that year. Why was this expenditure made?

It was in commemoration of confederation year. These peonies were sent from Canada to Great Britain, and were exhibited all over London and throughout the United Kingdom/ To show just how .well these peonies were preserved, they were sent over to London, were distributed from the railway offices, from Canada House and all the principal buildings in London and throughout the United Kingdom, and some of them arrived back in Canada in perfect condition after having crossed the ocean twice. I think that was money well spent. lit was one of the beet pieces of advertising that has been done for Canada.
Under vote 55 I notice an item for Canadian boys. I would like to know what percentage of this item wias spent last year, and what is proposed for this year.

None of this money has been spent. The department has been trying to make an arrangement with the different provincial government similar to that made with the Imperial government, and if the provincial governments would come through, I think that there would be no trouble in getting the Dominion parliament to meet them. The British boys are supposed to have saved $500, to have lived and worked on a farm, and must show that they were capable, industrious and intelligent. Then the
Sm ppl y-Immigra tion

British government will advance to tihem a loan of $1,250 and the Dominion government a like amount, making a total of $2,500, which with the $500 already saved gives the boy a capital of $3,000 on which to start farming. If the [DOT]provincial governments would come through and meet us in the same way as the Imperial government has done, I have no ' hesitation in saying that we would make a similar arrangement with them. I am longing for the time when we can do for the Canadian boy dxacbly what we are doing for the British boy.
Was there an item in the estimates last year for this same purpose?
Yes, but we have never been able to make an arrangement with the provincial governments.
No money has been spent?

No. There is a great deal of talk about the tremendous amount of money that has been spent on immigration and assisting people to come here, but all that we are spending in that direction is our share of the assisted passages for people who are going on farms. This government has never contributed one dollar of oash towards any settlement of land up to to-day.
I think it is very desirable to make that statement because the position is much misunderstood in the country. Perhaps the minister would amplify it.

When the British government offers a loan of $1,500 to the British boy if we will provide a like amount, it is very difficult to say that we will have nothing to do with it. A vast amount of money has come into this country and been spent under that scheme.
How much altogether?

I could not say offhand, but the deputy will look it up. We hear a great deal said about the large amount of money that is being spent on bringing people in from outside in comparison with what is being spent on the settlement of Canadians. What we are spending is for the assistance of these people after they come here, giving them assistance and advice along the lines the hon. member for Red Deer spoke about. I think the house has a wrong impression as to the amoumit of money that is being spent by the Canadian government to bring immigrants to this country. I want all the facts brought out. I have nothing to hide, and if the house does not like the facts-
You have a majority behind you anyway.
It seems rather difficult to get them in line this afternoon.

The minister said a while ago that if the provinces would come forward and provide loans for the Canadian boy as the Imperial government is doing for the British boy, the Dominion government would pay its share. What would be the position if an individual took the place of the province in putting up the amount of money required to settle Canadian boys? Would the Dominion government put up an equal amount?

subtopic: RIGHT OP MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill
brings before the house a very interesting question on constitutional law. The question is, have we the right to do something or not? What are the rights of this parliament, and what are the rights of the legislatures in each province?
Sometimes we have every sympathy for a sad case, or for some people who are in trouble. If a beggar goes to another man and says " I am destitute, I want some help, I badly need assistance," and the other man gives him a counterfeit one hundred dollar bill, that is no help at all for the beggar, because if he goes to a store and tries to change that bill the merchant will have him arrested and sent to gaol. The help, therefore, that we give to people must not be counterfeit help, so to speak, but help that really does assist. I heard some of my colleagues in the house relate some very sad divorce cases. For instance, the husband goes away and leaves his wife in charge of a family without any money. What can the wife do if the domicile of the husband is where he is, and if he does not happen to live in the country

Divorce Proceedings-Domicile
in which the couple had resided then where is the domicile, or where can the wife have a domicile in order that she may be able to take divorce proceedings against her husband?
There are some very sad cases indeed. But Canada has a constitution, granted by the imperial parliament, and we can help people who are in trouble only in accordance with our rights under that constitution. In order to know what kind of help we can give to people in such destitute circumstances, or to know whether we can give them any help at all, we must refer to the British North America Act, enacted by the imperial parliament in the year 1867. Section 92 of that act., paragraph 13, reads as follows:
Exclusive powers of provincial legislatures.
92. In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
13. Property and civil rights in the province.

speechtext:
I will tell you later what
happened at the interprovincial conference, and it will be a good lesson for you. Section 146 of the British North America Act, relating to the admission of other colonies into the Dominion, reads thus:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, on addresses from the Houses of the Parliament of Canada, and from the houses of the respective legislatures of the colonies or provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, to admit those colonies or provinces, or any of them, into the Union, and on address from the Houses of the Parliament of Canada to admit Rupert's land and the Northwestern Territory, or either of them, into the Union, on such terms and conditions in each case as are in the addresses expressed and as the queen thinks fit to approve, subject to the provisions of this act;-
"Subject to the provisions of this act," therefore subject to section 92.
-and the provisions of any order in council in that behalf shall have effect as if they had been enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
There is also the following provision in the British North America Act, 1871,	34-35
Victoria, chapter 28, section 4:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time make provision for the administration, peace, order, and good government of any territory not for the time being included in any province.
When the province of Prince Edward Island entered confederation the following address was passed, as found in the schedule to the order in council of Her Majesty in council admitting that province into the union in the year 1873:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects. . . . humbly approach Your Majesty for the purpose of representing:
That the constitution of the executive authority and of the legislature of Prince Edward Island shall, subject to the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, continue, as at the time of the union, until altered under the authority of the said act, and the House of Assembly of Prince Edward Island existing at the date of the union shall, unless sooner dissolved, continue for the period for which it was elected.
So that we see that even after confederation, after the British North America Act was passed, an order in council was issued by Her Majesty in council, in which reference is made to that act; and the statement appears that when Prince Edward Island entered the Canadian confederation it should be subject to the provisions of the British North America Act of 1867. It will be seen, therefore, that the constitution has not changed and that this parliament is vested with certain powere and rights exclusively, while the legislature of every province is similarly exclusively vested with peculiar rights and powers. But what is most important to know is the fact that in that part of the act which retfers to the powers and rights of the provinces there appear the words "ex* elusive" and "exclusively". This means that the provinces may do certain things which this parliament oannot do. And the fathers of confederation were wise when they incorporated those provisions in the act inasmuch as they obviate conflicts in law.
What member of this house will dare to say that domicile is not a question of civil right? Domicile is the place where a person, in the legal sense of the word, has- his place of business. The domicile of the head of a family is the place where that man is supposed to have permanent residence, the place where he lives all the time. Domicile comes from the Latin "domus," meaning a house or home. Domicile therefore is the place where a man has his home. A man has only one domicile, and it is not only the place where he can exercise civil rights under the law; it is also the place where he may be found when anyone wishes

to sue him in any case in which he is the defendant. Domicile is the place where he conducts his chief business and where he lives.
Now with regard to the family: the wife has the same domicile as her husband. I could cite some old precedents to that effect, not only from the history of the province of Quebec but also from that of England. For example, I could cite the case of Queen Marie Henriette of England, who was a daughter of Louis XIII. That queen of England was born in France where she lived for twenty-five years, and she was Queen of England when she died. Her heirs claimed the right to her estate, amounting to 100,000 crowns, and they would have been entitled thereto had the French law applied in England. But it was decided that she could not have any other domicile than that of her husband in England. This case is reported in Phillimore's Law of Domicile, pages 28 and 29.

Now I submit that the fact that domicile is a question of civil rights, the fact that the exercise of civil rights comes within the purview of the province exclusively, shows very clearly that even if we were of the same opinion as the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) it would be impossible to carry his point of view because we have no power to pass any such act.

It depends a great deal on intent to remain and to make the place where he happens to be his domicile.
Our divorce jurisdiction is operated under the laws of England as they stood. I think it was, in 1870, and the laws of England regarding divorce are indissolubly connected with our jurisdiction. I need1 not go back to the time of Louis and Catherine in order to refer to the case cited by my hon. friend, because we have more recent cases decided by the privy council, notably-Lord Advocate of Scotland versus Jaffray, which was followed in the Cook case. I view with a great deal of disfavour any attempt to make a special ruling in regard to the law of domicile. That is a matter of private international law or common law, and has been too well established to be interfered with lightly. As far as I know this is the first time 'that it has been proposed to pass legislation directly affecting what is or what is not to be a domicile. The law has grown up after years of consideration and I think it may be taken to be firmly established. The husband's domicile is the domicile of the wife, not only because

Divorce Proceedings-Domicile
she has agreed to live with him but because of the unity which came into effect with the marriage tie. I think the Jaffray case is perhaps the leading authority on this question. In that Case the domicile of the husband had been transferred1 to Australia, and notwithstanding the fact that a separation under the English law might have been ordered under the circumstances, and the court said that there was no reason why a divorce could not be obtained if the action had been taken in the proper place, that is Australia, the court saw no reason to interfere with the well established law applying to divorce by making any variation in that part of it which related to domicile.
It seems to me that the amendment is very loose, and I do not see how this house can pass it. Apparently it is proposed that for the purpose of securing a divorce-
