-for the purpose of securing a divorce a domicile may be obtained by the wife. She must be deserted by and live separate and apart from her husband for a period of at least two years, but the bill does not say how that is to be determined. I suppose an action will have to be taken or the matter settled in a legal tribunal to determine whether or not she has acquired a domipile and whether or not she has been deserted under the circumstances set out and has lived apart from her husband for a period of two years.

In petitions for divorce
it is a necessary part of the evidence to establish domicile. Under this particular act a separate domicile may be acquired by a married woman and it will be necessary for her in her action for divorce to establish, in the first place, that she has been deserted, and, in the second place, that she has acquired a separate domicile, in order to give the court jurisdiction to pronounce a decree of divorce.

I do no't think that anyone who has read the aict will doubt that it will be necessary for some tribunal to determine that the woman has acquired a domicile, a domicile for this one specific purpose. If my hon. friends had wanted to enable the wife to sue in certain jurisdictions, it seems to me that it might have been effected by leaving out all reference to domicile, and then it would have read:
-and lived separate and apart from her husband for a period of two years and upwards, and is still living separate and apart from her

husband, may commence an action for divorce in the province praying that her marriage may be dissolved, and that the courts of that province shall have full jurisdiction in the premises.
I view with a great deal of distrust any interference by statutory enactment with this well! established principle in divorce, because there are so many complications which might follow, such as successions after death and so on, and .it would be very difficult for us to guard against every (eventuality which might occur where the wife could be given by statute a particular domicile.
I do not think we are concerned with the question of whether or not it is a matter of civil rights. This house has jurisdiction in the matter of divorce. We have a bill here *which will give a domicile to a deserted wife in the place where she is living, and not in the plaice where her husband's domicile may be. We are not concerned with whether or not the provinces desire to assume the responsibility for enacting such legislation with regard to their own court.
Apart from all this, I would say that without any question this bill would simplify the obtaining of a divorce.
I do mot understand the attitude of my hon. friends opposite who profess that they do not want to see an increase in divorce in this country, but still object to giving the province of Ontario the right to have a divorce court. Everyone knows that where a divorce case is tried in open court, subject to all the rules of evidence and the careful scrutiny of same, there is very little likelihood of a divorce being granted in a mistaken case as may haipp'en before the Senate committee, rushed as it is. I do not agree with the actions of th-ait committee in many ways; I think it is overpressed and it is not a tribunal properly set up to look into the evidence and make a proper adjudication thereon. Each province should have its own divorce courts where these actions could be tried in the usual way, and, as I said before, I do not understand the attitude of my hon. friends opposite who, professing to a desire to restrict the elase with which a divorce .may be Obtained, still vote against a divorce court being established in the province of Ontario.
I agree thoroughly with them that we do not want anything which wil make it easier to obtain a divorce. In regard to the marriage tie there has grown up a sort of premeditated uncertainty which is endangering the social life of this country. I think we are making it much easier to obtain divorce by passing such a law as is here suggested, and for that reason, aside from the interference with the private international law and common law

Empire settlement scheme, including grants to immigration societies, provinces, women's hostels, etc., as may be authorized by the governor general in council, $1,000,000.

This appears to be quite an old item in the estimates, but I do not think it adds very much to Canadian immigration or benefits Canada in any way. I think the expenditure of $1,000,000 proposed here could be made to much better advantage on many other things in Canada, and I believe that the general opinion on this side of the house at least, and I believe throughout the country generally, is that assisted immigration is a mistake on the part of Canada. We have a good country here which naturally attracts people, and if we were to eliminate assistance to immigrants I think we would attract a more desirable class of people, increase our immigration and satisfy our own people to a greater extent than is the case with this assisted immigration.
I have discussed this matter on previous occasions, and while I do not expect many hon. members on this side of the bouse to support me, feeling perhaps that loyalty to their party is stronger than any other feeling at present, still I believe that if a free vote could be taken without any obligation to support the government or the minister in the matter, this item would be defeated by a very large majority. I have no criticism to make with regard to the present minister; I think perhaps he is doing as well as any minister could under the circumstances, but the time has arrived when Canada would be much better served by allowing healthy, energetic and enterprising young people to come here of their own accord instead of taxing the people of this country in order to assist what may be more or less undesirable class of people to come to Canada. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I would go so far as to say that we might abolish the Department of Immigration altogether without any great hardship to Canada. I think if we must have our present quota of ministers, a minister of

mines would serve a much better purpose thau a minister of immigration. Any restrictive measures necessary in connection with immigration could be undertaken by the Department of Justice and the medical inspection of immigrants could be looked after by the Department of Health. I believe if we entirely eliminated the Department of Immigration more people would seek' entrance to Canada than is the case to-day. I would even say that where we have caused a certain amount of hardship or grievance by the appointment of medical officers in Europe we might well withdraw those appointments and leave everyone free to come to Canada on an equal basis subject to our willingness to admit them. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I desire to move in amendment:
That vote No. 56 he reduced by three-fourths of $999,999.

I heartily support the amendment just moved, for reasons I have previously indicated and which I do not intend to repeat to-night. This afternoon we had consistency and logic preached to U3, and if I desire to be consistent and logical I must-support the amendment.
I should add that in supporting this amendment I do not impute any blame or criticism to the Minister of Immigration; we realize that he is an honest and capable man doing his level best with a bad job, but we do blame the policy, for which the minister is not responsible. He inherited that policy and he is trying to navigate as best he can with it, but in my humble judgment this policy is a misuse of the taxpayers' money. More than that it is useless, because we have been told that all the people whom we bring to Canada at such great cost do not stay here. For these reasons I desire to support the amendment.

While I am not perhaps
prepared to go the length to which my hon. friend from Pontiac wishes to go, in this item is included grants to provinces. I am prepared to leave out those grants, but in order to show that I heartily approve of the principle enunciated by the hon. member for Pontiac, namely that this government should no longer vote money for the assistance of immigrants, I am prepared to vote for his amendment. I firmly believe that the vast majority of the people of this country no longer wish any of the taxpayers' money to be expended in inducing people to come to Canada. If they wish to come here we should allow them to do so, provided we surround their entry with certain medical and moral safeguards but to have an agency in Europe 78594-1874
or in any part of the world to ask people to come here after describing to them in glowing terms the future they will have in this country I think is going altogether too far. I do not believe that ten per cent of the members of the house are prepared to get up and say that they desire more assisted immigrants in their own constituencies. I will say that we do not want any more in my constituency. The members rise in their seats and say that we must people the fertile plains of the west, but very few of them would be prepared to say that they have room in their own home towns or their own home cities for any more people from the other side.
Bring back the Canadian boys.

I would like to offer a word of explanation in regard to this vote. The total amount spent last year amounted to $034,(399.70. When we strike the estimate we have to allow for a sufficient amount to cover the total cost of the passages, but that amount is reduced by what is repaid by the British government.

As far as Canada was concerned, the total cost of the assisted passages amounted to $532,228, which is a long way from the $1,000,000 which many members seem to think we are paying for these passage grants. A grant of $20,640 was made to hostels and societies, and our share of the passage loans, which are recoverable, amounted to $16,693.17. That reduces the total expenditure for last year which will not be returned, to $618,592. I think a very careful analysis of the whole Immigration department activities by am expert accountant would be a very good thing, and if it is my luck to present the estimates another year I intend to have that done so that I will be able to show the house that the amount spent on immigration is very much smaller than the estimates would aptpear to indicate.
I would like to point out to the house what the imperial government is contributing to-

wards that amount. The figures I am giving include the whole period during which the Empire Settlement Act has been in force, the last six years. As Minister of Immigration I ha.d no connection with the bringing in of that act. It has been in force for six years and will inn out at the end of the present year. That would be the proper time to take such steps as are being taken here to-night. We have an agreement with the British government which we cannot repudiate and I do not think the hon. member who has moved the amendment realizes that fact.
When does that agreement expire?
The last day of the present year.
The fiscal or the calendar year?

It will be the calendar year. That would be the proper time to take such steps as are being taken at the present moment. This government has entered into a bargain with the imperial government which it is in honour bound obliged to carry out. The British government has paid, under this Empire Settlement Act, $4,105,977.43 in loans and passage grants. That expenditure was made in connection with the three thousand family scheme. That passage money will never be repaid, except the small amount which has been loaned, but the land grants will be recoverable. In all the British government has paid out in cash $9,105,977, and of that amount $5,000,000 will be recoverable from those brought out under the three thousand family scheme. I would like the committee to pay attention to this, because it is very important.

paying?

That has all been discussed
with hon. members on my hon. friend's side of the house.

If the minister is not more
closely in touch with the other offices in the United States than he is with the Detroit office, he should not discuss any of them, I notice some huge expenditures in maintaining offices in the United States. In one there are four clerks and in most of them there are one or two clerks and an immigration agent drawing S3,120 a year. Stenographers are maintained; in several offices there is only one, indicating that there is
very little work to be done, and I believe several of these offices could be closed without any loss to the Dominion. In view of the opinions that have been expressed to-night, the department should take heed and reduce these huge expenditures for maintaining offices in the United States.

Then the hon. gentleman is going.

There is a little difference in the two numbers, owing to the conditions under which they came in. The Canadian statement is 89,321 and the imperial government's is 87,284, a difference of about 2,000. The difference arises in the way some passage grants are paid. Actually 89,321 people came in.

There is just one question I should like to ask in connection with this vote and the amendment. I believe my views are pretty well known; at least, I endeavour to express them clearly. Am I correct in assuming that the larger part of this vote is already under commitment; that is, to fulfil commitments, either legal or moral, with the British government and other organizations, and that this money now is practically morally due; that 'is, that commitments have been entered into covering almost the full extent of the money, which commitments will not be discharged until the end of the present year?

The hon. member is quite correct. The people are coming in now and getting their passage money at reduced rates under this agreement. I do not think we can do anything but leave the estimate as it is for the present year.

That is what I think. A notice of motion as to a future year's policy might be quite in order, but I feel strongly on the question of the commitments we have entered into and I would hesitate very much before refusing to vote for money which we are almost bound in honour to pay, unless we are prepared to cancel the commitments we have made.

Would the minister tell the committee just how much we are indebted to the British government? Personally I should like to support the amendment before the committee, but I wish to know the actual extent of our commitments, because we cannot break our pledge if we are committed.

We have been carrying on since the month of January under the present year's estimates and we will carry on until the 31st December of this year. The amount will depend entirely upon the number of immigrants who come out under the assisted passage scheme.

Has the minister been
approached as to any extension of this agreement?

I am not going to promise ahead. I have listened to what has been said in the committee to-night, but I am not going to make any promise.

If the house was in session I would certainly consult it, but I might be called upon to take the responsibility when the house was not in session. It would be a matter for the government, not the minister, to decide! The minister, of course, has power to enter into an agreement, but from what I have learned and from what I have heard in the house to-night I would not be prepared to enter into any agreement with the British government unless it was an arrangement made with the Canadian government as such.

The minister has evidently heard the opinions that have been expressed here to-night. Before voting on this item I would like some definite information from him. Will he promise to consult the House of Commons before entering into an agreement similar to the one he now 'has?

If the house is in session it *can be done at the time. The hon. member knows my private opinion about this, and I do not 'think I should be called upon to make a statement as to what I am likely to do twelve mouths henlce. I think the hon. gentleman should be content with that answer. He is asking me to commit myself when I do not know what th'e circumstances will be in the future.
When was this arrangement entered into?
The reason I ask is this: If the minister intends to make a new arrangement, is he going to make it for one year or for six years, in view of the feeling of the house on this matter?

I do not think it is fair
for hon. gentlemen to seek to commit me as to what I shall do twelve months hence. I am responsible for what is taking place at the present time, and I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I attempted to say now what I shall do twelve months hence. I do not know what the circumstances will be then.
Would it be asking too much to ask the minister to consult this house before entering into another agreement?

I believe in parliamentary
government wherever possible.
Mr. NEI'LL: I find myself in a good deal of accord with the remarks of the two hon. gentlemen directly opposite. Apparently this is about the first time that some of the more remote members of the house have had a chance to express themselves on this immigra-

tion policy, and it is easy to see from the remarks that have been made that hon. gentlemen do not stand for a largely assisted immigration policy. I do not want to embarrass the government if they have made commitments that we must in good faith keep, but I entirely agree with the leader of the Progressive party that we are entitled to some statement, if we vote this money, as to whether we will be consulted before a similar policy is inaugurated in the future. The minister says that we must in good faith pass this estimate, but he can make the same remark next year or the year after. What I would suggest-I do not want to be put in the position of bartering with the government at all-would be that, if we pass this vote to relieve the government of the unpleasant position of having made commitments amid not being able to fulfill them, which we do not want to see, he will very seriously consider the feeling that has been exhibited here to-night and will consult this house before he goes into any extensive system of assisted immigration in the future. Speaking for my district, I have consistently opposed it and I know that that is the feeling of the people I represent. I came out in the steerage myself, unassisted, and nobody hand-fed or paip-fad me when I got here, I am quite wiling that other people should have similar opportunities.
